rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes the stated duration as the time from the youths’ death until the Qur’an revealed their story.
rows.anchor: قيل بعد موتهم إلى نزول القرآن فيهم، على قول مجاهد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the duration means until the youths died.
rows.anchor: أو إلى أن ماتوا على قول الضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation measures their time in the cave, the duration Jews had given with additions and omissions.
rows.anchor: بما لبثوا في الكهف، وهي المدة التي ذكرها الله تعالى عن اليهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God knows the duration, unless He has disclosed it to someone.
rows.anchor: أي لا يعلم علم ذلك إلا الله أو من علمه ذلك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah reads the phrase as an exclamation: none sees or hears better than God; the wording describes perception.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: لا أحد أبصر من الله ولا أسمع. وهذه عبارات عن الإدراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes the verbs as commands: by His revelation and guidance God showed the Prophet the truth and made the world hear it.
rows.anchor: بوحيه وإرشاده هداك وحججك والحق من الأمور، وأسمع به العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading means that God showed the youths and made them hear what He said about them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى أبصرهم وأسمعهم ما قال الله فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lack of any guardian may refer to the Cave Companions, whom only God protected.
rows.anchor: أي لم يكن لأصحاب الكهف ولي يتولى حفظهم دون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively it refers to disbelievers disputing the youths’ duration: they have no manager besides God, so cannot know without His disclosure.
rows.anchor: ما لهؤلاء المختلفين في مدة لبثهم ولي دون الله يتولى تدبير أمرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ya reading with a nominative kaf reports that God shares His judgment with none.
rows.anchor: قرىء بالياء ورفع الكاف، على معنى الخبر عن الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عامر والحسن وأبو رجاء وقتادة والجحدري
rows.claim: These readers use second-person ta with a still kaf, addressing the Prophet and coordinating the clause with the command to see and hear.
rows.anchor: بالتاء من فوق وإسكان الكاف على جهة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads the ya with a jussive; Yaqub says he does not know its grammatical basis.
rows.anchor: بالياء من تحت والجزم. قال يعقوب: لا أعرف وجهه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas said the youths had perished: near their cave he found bones and told his party they had vanished long ago.
rows.anchor: فوجدوا عظاما فقالوا: هذه عظام أهل الكهف. فقال لهم ابن عباس: أولئك قوم فنوا وعدموا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya cites a report that Jesus will perform pilgrimage with the Cave Companions, who have not yet made pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: ليحجن عيسى بن مريم ومعه أصحاب الكهف فإنهم لم يحجوا بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this account, the youths remain asleep rather than dead until shortly before the Hour; the author says scripture identifies Jesus as God’s servant and messenger and says he will pass al-Rawha as pilgrim or visitor.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا هم نيام ولم يموتوا إلى يوم القيامة، بل يموتون قبيل الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to recite may conclude the Cave story: follow the Qur’an, for God’s words cannot be changed and His account of the youths will not fail.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو من تمام قصة أصحاب الكهف أي اتبع القرآن فلا مبدل لكلمات الله ولا خلف فيما أخبر به

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari interprets the unchangeable words as God’s threats against sinners who oppose His Book.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: لا مغير لما أوعد بكلماته أهل معاصيه والمخالفين لكتابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Prophet does not follow the Qur’an and opposes it, he will find no refuge apart from God.
rows.anchor: ملتحدا } أي ملجأ. وقيل موئلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Multaḥad derives from inclination: one who seeks refuge has turned toward the place sought.
rows.anchor: وأصله الميل ومن لجأت إليه فقد ملت إليه

rows.speaker: القشيري أبو نصر عبد الرحيم
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri identifies this verse as the end of the Cave Companions’ story.
rows.anchor: قال القشيري أبو نصر عبد الرحيم: وهذا آخر قصة أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: When Muawiya wanted to uncover the cave, Ibn Abbas objected that God had barred someone better than him, citing the warning that an observer would flee; a wind drove out the men sent in.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: قد منع الله من هو خير منك عن ذلك

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabi also relates an elaborate report in which the Prophet sends Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali to the youths by a wind; they enter, convey his greeting, and the youths accept Islam before returning to sleep until the Mahdi and Resurrection.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سأل الله أن يريه إياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One chronology places the youths in the cave before Jesus, with their awakening in the interval between Jesus and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن أصحاب الكهف دخلوا الكهف قبل المسيح فأخبر الله تعالى المسيح بخبرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another says they lived before Moses, who mentioned them in the Torah, prompting the Jews’ question to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانوا قبل موسى عليه السلام وأن موسى ذكرهم في التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view places their cave entry after Jesus; the author leaves which chronology is correct to God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: دخلوا الكهف بعد المسيح فالله أعلم أي ذلك كان

rows.speaker: سلمان الفارسي
rows.claim: Salman reports that Uyaina ibn Hisn and al-Aqra ibn Habis asked the Prophet to move poor wool-clad Muslims such as Salman and Abu Dharr away so the notables could sit and learn from him.
rows.anchor: جاءت المؤلفة قلوبهم إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: عيينة بن حصن والأقرع بن حابس فقالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage from the recitation command through the warning of Hell was revealed in response; the Prophet found the poor worshippers remembering God and praised the command to stay with them in life and death.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا أصابهم في مؤخر المسجد يذكرون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those seeking God’s face are seeking His obedience.
rows.anchor: يريدون وجهه } أي طاعته

rows.speaker: نصر بن عاصم ومالك بن دينار وأبو عبد الرحمن
rows.claim: These readers recite the parallel command as do not expel those who call on their Lord at morning and evening, citing its spelling in the codex.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نصر بن عاصم ومالك بن دينار وأبو عبد الرحمن

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas says the codex spelling does not compel that reading, since life and prayer are also written with waw, and Arabs rarely say al-ghudwa because the time is already familiar.
rows.anchor: لا يلزم لكتبهم الحياة والصلاة بالواو، ولا تكاد العرب تقول الغدوة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan’s reported reading says do not let your eyes pass beyond them; al-Yazidi explains it as looking toward worldly people instead.
rows.anchor: إلى غيرهم من أبناء الدنيا طلبا لزينتها حكاه اليزيدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is not to look down on the poor, as when an eye recoils from someone it regards as contemptible.
rows.anchor: كما يقال فلان تنبو عنه العين أي مستحقرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told not to seek the adornment of worldly life by keeping company with the leaders who wanted the poor removed; he did not intend to do so, but God forbade it as a warning despite His protection of him from shirk.
rows.anchor: أي تتزين بمجالسة هؤلاء الرؤساء الذين اقترحوا إبعاد الفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tureed is a present-tense circumstantial verb, illustrated by Imru al-Qays’s use of a present verb in a circumstantial setting.
rows.anchor: فعل مضارع في موضع الحال أي لا تعد عيناك مريدا كقول امرىء القيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the claim that the verb must govern the eyes directly, the author explains the raised eyes as equivalent to their not turning away, with the command in meaning directed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: من رفع العينين يؤول إلى معنى النصب فيهما، إذ كان لا تعد عيناك عنهم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj clarifies that the command means not to turn the Prophet’s gaze from the poor toward people of status and adornment.
rows.anchor: لا تصرف بصرك عنهم إلى غيرهم من ذوي الهيئات والزينة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the warning about the heedless heart was revealed about Umayya ibn Khalaf, who wanted the poor kept away and Meccan nobles brought near; heedlessness means a heart sealed against monotheism.
rows.anchor: نزلت في أمية بن خلف الجمحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following one’s desire here means shirk.
rows.anchor: يعني الشرك. { وكان أمره فرطا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faraṭ may mean negligence and falling short through delaying faith, excess beyond bounds in boastful speech, or being first to do evil.
rows.anchor: من التفريط الذي هو التقصير وتقديم العجز بترك الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase God made his heart heedless may mean that He found it heedless, as in ordinary Arabic expressions that describe finding someone in a condition.
rows.anchor: وجدناه غافلا كما تقول: لقيت فلانا فأحمدته

rows.speaker: عبد الرزاق وسفيان الثوري
rows.claim: An alternative occasion identifies the heedless person as Uyaina ibn Hisn al-Fazari.
rows.anchor: في عيينة بن حصن الفزاري ذكره عبد الرزاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Haqq may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning say: it is the truth; alternatively it is a subject whose predicate is from your Lord.
rows.anchor: رفع على خبر الابتداء المضمر أي قل هو الحق. وقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God controls guidance and error: He guides or misleads whom He wills, and truth can be given to the weak and withheld from the rich; the Prophet is not to expel believers for the leaders’ preferences.
rows.anchor: فإليه التوفيق والخذلان، وبيده الهدى والضلال، يهدي من يشاء فيؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The invitation to believe or disbelieve is a threat, not permission to choose either without consequence: disbelief brings the prepared Fire, while faith brings the Garden.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا بترخيص وتخيير بين الإيمان والكفر، وإنما هو وعيد وتهديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿtadna means prepared, and the wrongdoers meant here are disbelievers who deny the truth.
rows.anchor: أي أعددنا. { للظالمين } أي للكافرين الجاحدين

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari defines a suradiq as a canopy stretched over a courtyard, and also uses it for a tent made of coarse hair; al-Ruʾba’s verse pictures glory as a canopy over its owner.
rows.anchor: قال الجوهري: السرادق واحد السرادقات التي تمد فوق صحن الدار

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrabi takes the fire’s suradiq as its enclosing wall.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: «سرادقها» سورها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the enclosure as a wall of fire.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: حائط من نار

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says a neck emerges from the Fire and surrounds disbelievers like an enclosure.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: عنق تخرج من النار فتحيط بالكفار كالحظيرة

rows.speaker: القتبي وابن عزيز
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybi and Ibn Aziz identify the suradiq as the surrounding curtain or barrier of a tent.
rows.anchor: القتبي: السرادق الحجزة التي تكون حول الفسطاط. وقاله ابن عزيز

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah says it is smoke enclosing the disbelievers, like the smoke described in the verses about a three-branched shade and black smoke.
rows.anchor: هو دخان يحيط بالكفار يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the enclosing barrier the sea surrounding the world.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه البحر المحيط بالدنيا

rows.speaker: يعلى بن أمية
rows.claim: Yaʿla ibn Umayya reports the Prophet called the sea Hell and recited this verse, saying he would neither enter nor be touched by a drop while alive.
rows.anchor: والله لا أدخلها أبدا ما دمت حيا ولا يصيبني منها قطرة

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid reports that the Fire’s canopy has four thick walls, each a forty-year journey; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan, sahih, gharib.
rows.anchor: لسرادق النار أربع جدر كثف كل جدار مسيرة أربعين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report indicates that the canopy is smoke or fire above the disbelievers, with walls as described.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن السرادق ما يعلو الكفار من دخان أو نار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says mahl is thick water like the dregs of oil.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: المهل ماء غليظ مثل دردي الزيت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies mahl as pus and blood.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: القيح والدم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak calls it black water, since Hell, its water, its trees, and its inhabitants are black.
rows.anchor: الضحاك: ماء أسود، وإن جهنم لسوداء، وماؤها أسود وشجرها أسود

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن مسعود
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda, with a similar report from Ibn Masud, describes molten metals of the earth boiling together as mahl.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: هو كل ما أذيب من جواهر الأرض من حديد ورصاص ونحاس

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says mahl is liquid at its hottest, and also describes it as a kind of tar; another view calls it poison. The author says these meanings are close.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: هو الذي قد انتهى حره

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Tirmidhi report compares the drink to oil lees and says the skin of the face falls when it is brought near; the compiler notes Rashdin was criticized for weak memory.
rows.anchor: إذا قربه إلى وجهه سقطت فروة وجهه

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: A report on the drink of pus says that when brought near it sears the face and scalp, and when swallowed cuts the intestines; al-Tirmidhi calls it gharib.
rows.anchor: يقرب إلى فيه فيكرهه فإذا أدني منه شوى وجهه ووقعت فروة رأسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports support the range of lexical interpretations, which the author says are all intended; Arabic dictionaries likewise record molten copper, lead, oil dregs, pus, and exudate.
rows.anchor: قلت: وهذا يدل على صحة تلك الأقوال، وأنها مرادة، والله أعلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes martefaqan as a place where people gather.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: معناه مجتمعا كأنه ذهب إلى معنى المرافقة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says martefaqan means a dwelling.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: منزلا

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata interprets it as a place of residence; another view calls it a bed, and al-Qutaybi a gathering place.
rows.anchor: عطاء: مقرا. وقيل مهادا. وقال القتبي: مجلسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These senses are close, and the root means a place to lean on an elbow; irtafaqa means to rest on the elbow.
rows.anchor: والمعنى متقارب وأصله من المتكأ، يقال منه: ارتفقت أي اتكأت على المرفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line uses irtafaqat in the sense of leaning or resting on the elbow.
rows.anchor: قالت له وارتفقت ألا فتى يسوق بالقوم غزالات الضحا

rows.speaker: أبو ذؤيب الهذلي
rows.claim: Abu Dhuʾayb says he spent the night resting on his elbow; ṣāb is the bitter sap of a tree.
rows.anchor: نام الخلي وبت الليل مرتفقا كأن عيني فيها الصاب مذبوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer rebukes and advises his companion: when entering the garden he should have said the words with his heart; the garden exists by God’s will, not his own power.
rows.anchor: أي بالقلب، وهو توبيخ ووصية من المؤمن للكافر ورد عليه

rows.speaker: الزجاج والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra explain the declaration as saying that the affair itself is what God wills.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج والفراء: الأمر ما شاء الله، أو هو ما شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative supplies the omitted answer: what God wills comes to be and what He does not will cannot be.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الجواب مضمر، أي ما شاء الله كان، وما لا يشاء لا يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wealth gathered in the garden came through God’s power, who could have removed its blessing; it was not the owner’s independent strength.
rows.anchor: فهو بقدرة الله تعالى وقوته لا بقدرتك وقوتك

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says anyone entering his home ought to say these words.
rows.anchor: قال أشهب قال مالك: ينبغي لكل من دخل منزله أن يقول هذا

rows.speaker: ابن وهب
rows.claim: Ibn Wahb says Hafs ibn Maysara saw the phrase written over Wahb ibn Munabbih’s door.
rows.anchor: قال ابن وهب قال لي حفص بن ميسرة: رأيت على باب وهب بن منبه مكتوبا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet taught Abu Musa that la hawla wa-la quwwata illa bi-llah is a treasure of Paradise; Muslim records the report in his Sahih with wording variants.
rows.anchor: لا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله إذا قالها العبد قال الله عز وجل أسلم عبدي واستسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report recommends saying in God’s name and acknowledging His will and power on entering or leaving home, saying this drives devils away and brings blessings; Aisha explains the angel’s responses as guidance, sufficiency, and protection.
rows.anchor: تنافرت عنه الشياطين من بين يديه وأنزل الله تعالى عليه البركات

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that one who says the invocation when leaving home is told he is guided, sufficed, and protected; al-Tirmidhi calls this route gharib, and Abu Dawud adds the three responses.
rows.anchor: من قال يعني إذا خرج من بيته باسم الله توكلت على الله لا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Ibn Majah’s report says two assigned angels answer each phrase as guidance, protection, or sufficiency, and the person’s two companions ask what they could want from one so provided for.
rows.anchor: إذا خرج الرجل من باب بيته أو باب داره كان معه ملكان موكلان به

rows.speaker: ابن خزيمة
rows.claim: Ibn Khuzayma explains the person released from power as someone who says this twenty or fifty times a day.
rows.anchor: الذي يبرىء نفسه من الحول والقوة يعني في اليوم عشرين مرة أو خمسين مرة

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas attributes protection from the evil eye to saying the phrase when something is admired.
rows.anchor: من رأى شيئا فأعجبه فقال ما شاء الله لا قوة إلا بالله لم يضره عين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A maxim says that whoever accepts whatever God wills will be content with what befalls him.
rows.anchor: ما من أحد قال ما شاء الله كان فأصابه شيء إلا رضي به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report assigns four protections to four phrases: the garden phrase against the evil eye, reliance on God against Satan, entrusting one’s affair to God against people’s plots, and the plea of Jonah against grief.
rows.anchor: من قال أربعا أمن من أربع: من قال هذه أمن من العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the conditional sentence, tara is jussive and fa-ʿasa is the answer; ana is parenthetical, or may emphasize the first-person pronoun as an object.
rows.anchor: شرط «ترن» مجزوم به، والجواب

rows.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: Isa ibn Umar reads ana with nominative case as a subject and aqalla as its predicate; the phrase is the second object, and retaining the yāʾ is good and original though its deletion is indicated by the kasra.
rows.anchor: والمفعول الأول النون والياء إلا أن الياء حذفت لأن الكسرة تدل عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-ʿasa means perhaps; the good promised instead of the garden may be in the Hereafter or, according to another view, in this world.
rows.anchor: أي فلعل ربي. { أن يؤتين خيرا من جنتك } أي في الآخرة

rows.speaker: الأخفش والقتبي وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: They say ḥusbānan means projectiles from the sky, with ḥusbāna as singular; Ibn al-Aʿrabi adds meanings such as cloud, cushion, or thunderbolt, and dictionaries also give torment, locusts, and reckoning.
rows.anchor: أي مرامي من السماء، واحدها حسبانة قاله الأخفش والقتبي وأبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥīṭa bi-thamarihi has an implicit verbal noun as its grammatical subject, though the genitive form may also be construed as nominative; the whole fortune was destroyed, fulfilling the companion’s warning.
rows.anchor: اسم ما لم يسم فاعله مضمر، وهو المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He turns his hands over in regret; alternatively, he turns over his dominion and sees nothing left to compensate what he spent, since hand can mean ownership.
rows.anchor: أي فأصبح الكافر يضرب إحدى يديه على الأخرى ندما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asbaḥa indicates the destruction happened at night, as in the story of the garden visited while its owners slept and left blackened by morning.
rows.anchor: على أن هذا الإهلاك جرى بالليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāwiyat ʿalā ʿurūshihā describes it as empty and fallen upon its roofs; the root can describe stars setting, barren land, or a collapsed house.
rows.anchor: أي خالية قد سقط بعضها على بعض مأخوذ من خوت النجوم تخوى خيا أمحلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden fell onto its trellises, destroying both crop and structure; this great calamity answers his transgression.
rows.anchor: فجمع عليه بين هلاك الثمر والأصل، وهذا من أعظم الجوائح، مقابلة على بغيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He wishes he had not associated anyone with his Lord, now recognizing that his blessings came from God’s power; the regret comes too late.
rows.anchor: أي يا ليتني عرفت نعم الله علي، وعرفت أنها كانت بقدرة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water-and-plant example is directed at the arrogant leaders who asked that poor believers be expelled; the earth’s plants grow lush after rain and then fade.
rows.anchor: أي صف لهؤلاء المتكبرين الذين سألوك طرد فقراء المؤمنين مثل الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plant may be said to mix through the water until flourishing, or to mix with one another after rain, since rain makes vegetation abundant.
rows.anchor: حتى استوى. وقيل: إن النبات اختلط بعضه ببعض حين نزل عليه الماء

rows.speaker: الحكماء
rows.claim: The sages compare worldly life with water because neither stays fixed, water vanishes as life does, and no one enters worldly life without exposure to its trials and harms.
rows.anchor: إنما شبه تعالى الدنيا بالماء لأن الماء لا يستقر في موضع، كذلك الدنيا لا تبقى على واحد

rows.speaker: الحكماء
rows.claim: Water in the right measure benefits, while excess destroys; likewise enough of worldly goods helps and surplus harms.
rows.anchor: لأن الماء إذا كان بقدر كان نافعا منبتا، وإذا جاوز المقدار كان ضارا مهلكا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A man asking to be among the successful is told to leave worldly life and take from it like still water: little suffices and much intoxicates.
rows.anchor: ذر الدنيا وخذ منها كالماء الراكد فإن القليل منها يكفي والكثير منها يطغي

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Muslim reports the Prophet saying successful is the one who submits, receives enough, and is made content with what God gives.
rows.anchor: قد أفلح من أسلم ورزق كفافا وقنعه الله بما آتاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hashīm is dry, broken, crumbling vegetation after water stops; the root also describes dry wood, a generous person, a weak body, showing affection, milking a camel, and crumbling bread.
rows.anchor: أي متكسرا من اليبس متفتتا، يعني بانقطاع الماء عنه، فحذف ذلك إيجازا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبعرى
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zibara’s verse praises Amr al-Ula for crumbling bread to feed Mecca’s lean, famine-struck people; Hashim’s name came from breaking and serving the bread after a famine.
rows.anchor: عمرو العلا هشم الثريد لقومه ورجال مكة مسنتون عجاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author recounts how Hashim brought bread and camels from Syria, crumbled the bread into pots, and fed Mecca during years of hardship, earning the name Hashim.
rows.anchor: فخرج هاشم إلى الشأم فأمر بخبز كثير فخبز له، فحمله في الغرائر على الإبل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة وابن كيسان وابن عباس
rows.claim: They gloss tadhruhu as dispersing, scattering, carrying to and fro, or turning about; the author says the senses are close.
rows.anchor: قاله أبو عبيدة. ابن قتيبة: تنسفه. ابن كيسان: تذهب به وتجيء

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف وابن عباس
rows.claim: Talha reads tadhrihi al-riḥ, and the codex of Ibn Masud likewise has tadhrihi; forms of the verb mean that wind carries something off.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي: وفي قراءة عبد الله

rows.speaker: سيبويه والفراء
rows.claim: A line cited by Sibawayh and al-Farra uses the verb for wind blowing a bird off course, illustrating the sense of scattering.
rows.anchor: فقلت له صوب ولا تجهدنه فيذرك من أخرى القطاة فتزلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is fully able to originate, annihilate, and bring things to life.
rows.anchor: من الإنشاء والإفناء والإحياء، سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people left to surge into one another may be all jinn and humans at Resurrection, or Gog and Magog at the time the barrier is completed, or after it opens as their multitude mingles in this world.
rows.anchor: لله تعالى أي تركنا الجن والإنس يوم القيامة يموج بعضهم في بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The middle view, placing this among Gog and Magog when the barrier is complete, is most apparent; the final view is most remote, while the first is also apt because Resurrection was just mentioned.
rows.anchor: أظهرها أوسطها، وأبعدها آخرها، وحسن الأول لأنه تقدم ذكر القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wave image describes bewilderment and fearful confusion, like waves of the sea surging against one another.
rows.anchor: واستعارة الموج لهم عبارة عن الحيرة وتردد بعضهم في بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blowing in the Trumpet here is the second blowing, with discussion given earlier in al-Anʿam.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { ونفخ في الصور } تقدم في «الأنعام»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gathers jinn and humans in the courts of Resurrection and openly displays Hell to the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: يعني الجن والإنس في عرصات القيامة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their eyes are covered from remembrance in the sense that they fail to see God’s signs and proofs; they are as if deaf and unable to bear His speech.
rows.anchor: أي هم بمنزلة من عينه مغطاة فلا ينظر إلى دلائل الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afa-ḥasiba can mean did they think; alternatively, a variant read with a still sin and ḍamma on bāʾ means did it suffice them.
rows.anchor: بإسكان السين وضم الباء أي كفاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s servants taken as protectors besides Him are Jesus, the angels, and Ezra; the omitted thought is whether they will avoid punishment or benefit from them.
rows.anchor: يعني عيسى والملائكة وعزيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses show that people may work while imagining their deeds good even though their effort is nullified; the cause is corrupt belief or ostentation, and here specifically disbelief.
rows.anchor: فيه دلالة على أن من الناس من يعمل العمل وهو يظن أنه محسن وقد حبط سعيه

rows.speaker: سعد
rows.claim: In a Bukhari report, Saʿd says the worst losers are Jews and Christians, not the Khawarij: Jews denied Muhammad, and Christians denied Paradise’s food and drink; he called the Khawarij covenant-breakers and wicked.
rows.anchor: أهم الحرورية؟ قال: لا هم اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question rebukes disbelievers who worship other than God: their efforts and hopes fail, making them the greatest losers in deeds.
rows.anchor: الآية معناها التوبيخ أي قل لهؤلاء الكفرة الذين عبدوا غيري

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies them as the disbelievers of Mecca.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد كفار أهل مكة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali identifies the worst losers as the Khawarij of Harura; on another occasion he names the monks in their cells, and tells Ibn al-Kawwa that he and his companions are meant.
rows.anchor: وقال علي: هم الخوارج أهل حروراء. وقال مرة: هم الرهبان أصحاب الصوامع

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says these identifications are weakened by the following description of people who disbelieved God’s signs and meeting Him; that fits Meccan idolaters, though Ali and Saʿd named groups that share aspects of the warning.
rows.anchor: فحبطت أعمالهم } وليس من هذه الطوائف من يكفر بالله ولقائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who believe and do good works will be given love in the hearts of God’s servants.
rows.anchor: أي حبا في قلوب عباده

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Saʿd and Abu Hurayra says that when God loves a servant He tells Gabriel, who announces it in heaven, and love is then placed for the servant on earth; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan sahih, and Bukhari, Muslim, and Malik give it by meaning.
rows.anchor: إذا أحب الله عبدا نادى جبريل إني قد أحببت فلانا فأحبه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas transmits a report that God gives believers affection, grace, and love in the hearts of the righteous and the nearest angels, then recites the verse.
rows.anchor: إن الله أعطى المؤمن الألفة والملاحة والمحبة في صدور الصالحين والملائكة المقربين

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Bara ibn Azib reports that the verse descended after the Prophet told Ali to ask God for a covenant with Him and affection in believers’ hearts.
rows.anchor: روى البراء بن عازب قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لعلي بن أبي طالب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse was revealed about Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, whom God made beloved and respected among believers, polytheists, and hypocrites.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: نزلت في عبد الرحمن بن عوف جعل الله تعالى له في قلوب العباد مودة

rows.speaker: هرم بن حيان
rows.claim: Harm ibn Hayyan says that whoever turns his heart toward God will find God turning believing hearts toward him with affection and mercy.
rows.anchor: وكان هرم بن حيان يقول: ما أقبل أحد بقلبه على الله تعالى إلا أقبل الله تعالى بقلوب أهل الإيمان إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says believers will be given affection in the hearts of believers and angels on the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يجعل الله تعالى لهم مودة في قلوب المؤمنين والملائكة يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says one loved in this life will also be loved in the next: God loves only a pious believer and is pleased only with the sincere and pure.
rows.anchor: إذا كان محبوبا في الدنيا فهو كذلك في الآخرة فإن الله تعالى لا يحب إلا مؤمنا تقيا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Muslim’s report from Abu Hurayra expands the sequence: God’s love prompts Gabriel and the heavens to love the servant, acceptance is placed on earth, and hatred likewise spreads when God hates a servant.
rows.anchor: إذا أحب عبدا دعا جبريل عليه السلام فقال: إني أحب فلانا فأحبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning addresses Meccans: should the ruins they pass while traveling and trading not teach them how earlier peoples were destroyed and make them fear the same fate?
rows.anchor: يريد أهل مكة أي أفلم يتبين لهم خبر من أهلكنا قبلهم من القرون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسلمي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Sulami, and others read the verb with nūn, nahd, which the author calls clearer.
rows.anchor: بالنون وهي أبين. و«يهد» بالياء مشكل لأجل الفاعل

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufans make kam the subject of the ya reading; al-Nahhas rejects this because an interrogative kam cannot be governed by what precedes it.
rows.anchor: وهذا خطأ لأن «كم» استفهام فلا يعمل فيها ما قبلها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the verb as the event of destroying earlier peoples guiding them; the actual subject is guidance, while kam is the object of ahlakna.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: المعنى أولم يهد لهم الأمر بإهلاكنا من أهلكنا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The syntax places an appointed term before the clause; without the prior decree and appointed term, punishment would have bound them. Lizam means binding punishment and kana has an omitted subject.
rows.anchor: فيه تقديم وتأخير أي ولولا كلمة سبقت من ربك وأجل مسمى لكان لزاما قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj makes the appointed term coordinate with the prior word or decree.
rows.anchor: مسمى } عطف على «كلمة»

rows.speaker: قتادة والقتبي
rows.claim: They identify the appointed term as Resurrection; another interpretation makes it their postponement until the Battle of Badr.
rows.anchor: قتادة: والمراد القيامة وقاله القتبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is commanded to endure their accusations that he is a sorcerer, soothsayer, or liar, knowing their punishment has a fixed time.
rows.anchor: أمره تعالى بالصبر على أقوالهم: إنه ساحر إنه كاهن إنه كذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the patience command was abrogated by the fighting verse; others say it remains, since fighting did not annihilate all disbelievers.
rows.anchor: ثم قيل: هذا منسوخ بآية القتال. وقيل: ليس منسوخا

rows.speaker: أكثر المتأولين
rows.claim: Most commentators take the prayer references as the five daily prayers: dawn before sunrise, afternoon before sunset, night prayer in the night hours, and Maghrib and noon at the day’s extremities.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر المتأولين: هذه إشارة إلى الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of day’s extremities counts the shared boundary at noon for both halves; Ibn Furak notes this analysis.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النهار ينقسم قسمين فصلهما الزوال، ولكل قسم طرفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation treats day as a generic recurring unit, so the plural extremities reflects each day having an end.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النهار للجنس فلكل يوم طرف، وهو إلى جمع لأنه يعود في كل نهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anāʾ al-layl means its hours; its singular has several forms, ini, inā, and anā.
rows.anchor: «وآناء الليل» ساعاته وواحد الآناء إني وإنى وأنى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says the command refers to voluntary prayer.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: المراد بالآية صلاة التطوع قاله الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa on the tāʾ, tarḍā means that the Prophet may be rewarded until content; al-Kisaʾi and Abu Bakr from Asim read the passive with ḍamma, meaning given what pleases him.
rows.anchor: } بفتح التاء أي لعلك تثاب على هذه الأعمال بما ترضى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is a nominative subject, and the clause ends at inqalaba ʿalā wajhihi on the common reading; the passage describes hypocrites.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية خبر عن المنافقين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns Shayba ibn Rabiʿa, who had become Muslim before the Prophet’s mission and apostatized when revelation came.
rows.anchor: يريد شيبة بن ربيعة كان قد أسلم قبل أن يظهر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid reports that a Jewish convert who lost his sight, wealth, and children asked the Prophet to release him from Islam; the Prophet said Islam smelts away impurity as fire purifies metals, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: أسلم رجل من اليهود فذهب بصره وماله فتشاءم بالإسلام فأتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a man judged the religion good when his wife bore a son and his horses foaled, but bad when neither happened.
rows.anchor: كان الرجل يقدم المدينة فإن ولدت امرأته غلاما ونتجت خيله قال هذا دين صالح

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators say Bedouins came to the Prophet, stayed Muslim when they prospered, and apostatized when hardship struck.
rows.anchor: نزلت في أعراب كانوا يقدمون على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فيسلمون فإن نالوا رخاء أقاموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other identifications are al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and, according to Ibn Zayd and others, the hypocrites.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزلت في النضر بن الحارث. وقال ابن زيد وغيره: نزلت في المنافقين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and others gloss worshipping on an edge as worship based on doubt; literally it describes someone unstable at an edge.
rows.anchor: على شك قاله مجاهد وغيره. وحقيقته أنه على ضعف في عبادته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes it one-sided worship: they worship in prosperity but not adversity; gratitude in good times and patience in hardship would mean serving God on both sides.
rows.anchor: أي على وجه واحد، وهو أن يعبده على السراء دون الضراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may also mean worship on condition: Shayba asked the Prophet for wealth, animals, and children before believing; after receiving and then losing them as a test, he apostatized.
rows.anchor: على شرط وذلك أن شيبة بن ربيعة قال للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says this is a hypocrite who worships with his tongue but not his heart; in general such a person is not wholly committed.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هو المنافق يعبد الله بلسانه دون قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When health and prosperity come, he is pleased and stays in the faith; when tried by hardship he turns back to his former disbelief, losing both worlds.
rows.anchor: صحة جسم ورخاء معيشة رضي وأقام على دينه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وحميد بن قيس والأعرج والزهري وابن أبي إسحاق ويعقوب
rows.claim: They read khāsir al-dunyā with an alif as an accusative circumstantial form, so there is no pause at wajhihi; his worldly loss is no share in spoils or praise, and his loss in the next life is no reward.
rows.anchor: نصبا على الحال، وعليه فلا يوقف على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion returns to idolaters who persist in denying resurrection; when death comes they see the angels taking their souls and realize their error, as in the account of angels seizing disbelievers.
rows.anchor: تيقن ضلالته وعاين الملائكة التي تقبض روحه كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ask to be returned so they can do the good they neglected; the words may have been spoken only inwardly.
rows.anchor: تمنى الرجعة كي يعمل صالحا فيما ترك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural imperative addressing God may magnify the addressee; Ibn Jurayj says they first call on God, then address the angels to return them to this world.
rows.anchor: وقيل: استغاثوا بالله عز وجل أولا، فقال قائلهم: رب، ثم رجع إلى مخاطبة الملائكة

rows.speaker: المزني
rows.claim: Another explanation takes irjiʿūn as repetition meaning return me again and again, like the reading of al-Muzani’s explanation of the command to throw into Hell.
rows.anchor: على جهة التكرير أي ارجعني ارجعني ارجعني وهكذا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the request is made by the people of shirk; the author adds that believers also ask for return, as discussed at the end of al-Munafiqun.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: المراد به أهل الشرك. قلت: ليس سؤال الرجعة مختصا بالكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request indicates that before death people know with certainty whether they belong to God’s allies or enemies, since otherwise they would not ask to return.
rows.anchor: ودلت الآية على أن أحدا لا يموت حتى يعرف اضطرارا أهو من أولياء الله أم من أعداء الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains what was left behind as the testimony that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد أشهد أن لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may mean acts of worship he neglected, or the wealth he left that he could have given in charity; laʿalla signals uncertainty about being returned or enabled to act if returned.
rows.anchor: أي فيما ضيعت وتركت العمل به من الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā rejects the presumed return: his plea will be thrown away; even if returned, he would not fulfill the promise, as the verse about their return says.
rows.anchor: هذه كلمة رد أي ليس الأمر على ما يظنه من أنه يجاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words may instead refer to God: His promise cannot fail, and He has said no soul is delayed past its term and that this disbeliever will not believe; alternatively the dying person utters them, but they do not help.
rows.anchor: ترجع إلى الله تعالى أي لا خلف في خبره

rows.speaker: الضحاك ومجاهد وابن زيد
rows.claim: They define barzakh as a barrier between death and Resurrection; Mujahid also calls it the barrier between death and return to earthly life.
rows.anchor: أي حاجز بين الموت والبعث قاله الضحاك ومجاهد وابن زيد

rows.speaker: الضحاك وابن عباس والسدي وقتادة وابن عيسى والكلبي
rows.claim: Further definitions are the interval between worlds, a veil, a term, what remains of worldly life, respite until Resurrection, or the period between the two trumpet blasts, said to be forty years; the author calls these close.
rows.anchor: وعن الضحاك: هو ما بين الدنيا والآخرة. ابن عباس: حجاب. السدي: أجل

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari defines barzakh as a barrier; the author says every barrier between two things is a barzakh and every dead person enters the interval from death to Resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال الجوهري: البرزخ الحاجز بين الشيئين

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi corrects a man who says the deceased has joined the next life: he has entered barzakh, neither this world nor the next.
rows.anchor: فقال: لم يصر من أهل الآخرة، ولكنه صار من أهل البرزخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The time word is annexed to they are raised because it is a time adverb, with the annexation expressing the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: لأنه ظرف زمان، والمراد بالإضافة المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trumpet here is the second blowing.
rows.anchor: المراد بهذا النفخ النفخة الثانية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says people will neither boast of family descent nor ask one another about tribe and lineage, and they will not recognize one another because terror overwhelms them.
rows.anchor: لا يفتخرون بالأنساب في الآخرة كما يفتخرون بها في الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: An alternative places this at the first blowing, when all creatures swoon; at the second they rise and ask one another. Explaining the apparent conflict with 37:50, Ibn Abbas says no living person remains after the first, while questioning occurs after entering Paradise.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أن ذلك في النفخة الأولى حين يصعق من في السموات ومن في الأرض

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says this verse concerns the second blowing.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: إنما عنى في هذه الآية النفخة الثانية

rows.speaker: أبو عمر زاذان
rows.claim: Abu Umar Zadhan recounts that when he complained to Ibn Masud that his foreign origin kept him from access, Ibn Masud drew him close and described the Day of Judgment, when a caller summons people owed rights; a woman rejoices at a claim against relatives.
rows.anchor: دخلت على ابن مسعود فوجدت أصحاب الخير واليمنة قد سبقوني إليه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: In the same report, God orders people’s rights restored; since worldly wealth is gone, good deeds are distributed to claimants, and the verse denies the usefulness of family ties then.
rows.anchor: فيقول: يا رب قد فنيت الدنيا فمن أين أوتيهم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The report continues that a person devoted to God who has even a mustard seed of good deeds has them multiplied and enters Paradise, citing the verse that God does not wrong an atom’s weight.
rows.anchor: إن الله لا يظلم مثقال ذرة وإن تك حسنة يضاعفها

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: If the person is wretched and has no good deeds left while creditors remain, the angels transfer their misdeeds to him and issue his writ to Hell.
rows.anchor: وإن كان شقيا قالت الملائكة: رب فنيت حسناته وبقي طالبون

none: The segment only says that discussion of these two verses has already occurred.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may ask how long they remained in their graves or how long they lived on earth; it is posed to disbelievers in the courts of Resurrection or in Hell.
rows.anchor: قيل: يعني في القبور. وقيل: هو سؤال لهم عن مدة حياتهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for years is read with fatḥa on the nūn as a sound masculine plural, though some Arabs inflect it with kasra and tanwīn.
rows.anchor: بفتح النون على أنه جمع مسلم، ومن العرب من يخفضها وينونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may forget their time in the graves from the terror of punishment, or because torment was suspended between the two trumpet blasts; a comparison says those killed by or dying in a prophet’s presence are punished until the first blast, then held as still as water until the second.
rows.anchor: أنساهم شدة العذاب مدة مكثهم في القبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they deem both worldly life and the grave interval brief beside what now faces them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: استقصروا مدة لبثهم في الدنيا وفي القبور ورأوه يسيرا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah says al-ʿāddīn are the people who count and know the duration; Mujahid says they are angels who were with people in the world.
rows.anchor: الذين يعرفون ذلك فإنا قد نسيناه

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read qul kam, an imperative: it may command the audience to say the answer, direct an angel to ask, or tell the Prophet to ask the disbeliever.
rows.anchor: على الأمر. ويحتمل ثلاثة معان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readers use qal as a report that God or the angels asked them how long they remained.
rows.anchor: على الخبر أي قال الله تعالى لهم، أو قالت الملائكة لهم كم لبثتم

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi also read qal in the clause, while the other readers report it; the stay is short because even a long grave interval is finite and brief beside endless Hell.
rows.anchor: ما لبثتم في الأرض إلا قليلا وذلك أن مكثهم في القبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse presents another proof of God’s power and asks whether one sees with the eye of the heart.
rows.anchor: ذكر من حججه شيئا آخر أي ألم تر بعيني قلبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yuzjī means to drive or guide along; Arabic uses it for wind driving clouds, a cow driving her calf, and easily collected tax.
rows.anchor: أي يسوق إلى حيث يشاء. والريح تزجي السحاب

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nabigha’s lines use azjī and tuzjī for leading along a remnant of life and driving snow clouds with the north wind.
rows.anchor: إني أتيتك من أهلي ومن وطني أزجي حشاشة نفس ما بها رمق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clouds are joined as they form so they grow connected and dense; the basic verb is hamzated, though a lightened waw reading is reported.
rows.anchor: أي يجمعه عند انتشائه ليقوى ويتصل ويكثف

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج والأصمعي
rows.claim: Though cloud is singular in form, baynahu can refer to its collective meaning or to its many parts; al-Asmaʿi rejects this and prefers the reading that names the two places.
rows.anchor: فكيف جاز بينه؟ فالجواب أن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rukām means piled together in layers, as in the piled cloud of another verse; the root means collecting one thing upon another.
rows.anchor: أي مجتمعا، يركب بعضه بعضا كقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو الأشهب العقيلي
rows.claim: Abu al-Ashhab al-Uqayli interprets wadq as lightning, supported by a poetic comparison of dust emerging like wadq from cloud openings.
rows.anchor: قولان: أحدهما: أنه البرق قاله أبو الأشهب العقيلي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most commentators say wadq is rain, and lines by an unnamed poet and Imru al-Qays use it for falling drops and rain.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أنه المطر قاله الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khilāl is the plural of khalal, the gaps and channels from which rain comes; the word also means being among a group.
rows.anchor: وخلال جمع خلل مثل الجبل والجبال، وهي فرجه ومخارج القطر منه

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says clouds are a sieve for rain; without them, water falling from the sky would ruin what it struck on earth.
rows.anchor: أن كعبا قال: إن السحاب غربال المطر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وأبو العالية
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Abu al-Aliya read khilal in the singular form khalal.
rows.anchor: وأبو العالية «من خلله» على التوحيد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: One explanation has mountains of hail in the sky, from which hail descends, with the omitted object supplied; al-Farra can treat the mountains themselves as hail.
rows.anchor: قيل: خلق الله في السماء جبالا من برد، فهو ينزل منها بردا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings say God created mountains in the sky that contain hail, or that hail descends in an amount or likeness of mountains; the repeated min can mark origin, partitive sense, and material.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن الله تعالى خلق في السماء جبالا فيها برد فيكون التقدير

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats both min before mountains and min before hail as extra, parsing mountains and hail as objects: hail descends like mountains.
rows.anchor: زائدة في الموضعين، والجبال والبرد في موضع نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hail strikes whom God wills as a punishment and is turned away from whom He wills as a blessing; a report says a particular glorification on hearing thunder protects from harm.
rows.anchor: فتكون إصابته نقمة، وصرفه نعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lightning’s brilliance almost takes sight; sanna is the brightness of the cloud’s lightning.
rows.anchor: أي ضوء ذلك البرق الذي في السحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sana in the short form means lightning’s flash and is also the name of a medicinal plant; the long form sanāʾ means elevation, though both share the sense of shining.
rows.anchor: فالسنا مقصور ضوء البرق. والسنا أيضا نبت يتداوى به

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Talha reads the long form sanāʾ for intense brightness and purity; al-Mubarrad distinguishes short-form flash from long-form rank and honor.
rows.anchor: على المبالغة في شدة الضوء والصفاء فأطلق عليه اسم الشرف

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Talha’s other reading, sanāʾ barqihi, is said by Ahmad ibn Yahya to use a plural of barqa, a flash or measure of lightning.
rows.anchor: قال أحمد بن يحيى: وهو جمع برقة. قال النحاس: البرقة المقدار من البرق

rows.speaker: الجحدري وابن القعقاع
rows.claim: They read yudhhibu in form IV, with bāʾ extra; the rest read yadhhabu, with bāʾ indicating attachment to the eyes.
rows.anchor: بضم الياء وكسر الهاء من الإذهاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lightning signals dense clouds and likely heavy rain while warning of possible lightning strikes.
rows.anchor: والبرق دليل على تكاثف السحاب، وبشير بقوة المطر، ومحذر من نزول الصواعق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning night and day may mean their alternation, their waxing and waning, changes between cloud-darkness and sun or moonlight, or shifts in the good, evil, benefit, and harm occurring in them.
rows.anchor: قيل: تقليبهما أن يأتي بأحدهما بعد الآخر. وقيل: تقليبهما نقصهما وزيادتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These changes in night, day, rain, and seasons are a lesson for people of insight.
rows.anchor: أحوال المطر والصيف والشتاء { لعبرة } أي اعتبارا { لأولي الأبصار } أي لأهل البصائر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda defines khilfa as one thing following another, as night and day each succeed the other; the word can describe alternating bodily positions or new plant leaves.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: الخلفة كل شيء بعد شيء. وكل واحد من الليل والنهار يخلف صاحبه

rows.speaker: زهير بن أبي سلمى
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s verse uses khilfa for successive groups of gazelles and their young appearing from hiding places.
rows.anchor: بها العين والآرام يمشين خلفة وأطلاؤها ينهضن من كل مجثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second poem illustrates a woman who shifts seasonally between her winter and summer homes, with successive settings described as khilfa.
rows.anchor: خلفة حتى إذا ارتبعت سكنت من جلق بيعا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid understands khilfa as opposition or difference, such as white and black; the author says the succession meaning is stronger.
rows.anchor: من الخلاف هذا أبيض وهذا أسود والأول أقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations are alternation in light and darkness and in increase and decrease, or an omitted phrase meaning that night and day possess difference.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يتعاقبان في الضياء والظلام والزيادة والنقصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation lets people remember and reflect that God did not create it in vain, and thank Him using their reason, thought, and understanding.
rows.anchor: فيعلم أن الله لم يجعله كذلك عبثا فيعتبر في مصنوعات الله

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: They explain the verse as allowing anyone who missed a good deed by night to make it up by day, and anyone who missed one by day to make it up by night.
rows.anchor: وقال عمر بن الخطاب وابن عباس والحسن: معناه من فاته شيء من الخير بالليل أدركه بالنهار

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A sound report says that a person whose customary night prayer is overtaken by sleep may pray after sunrise before noon and receive the night prayer’s reward, with the sleep counted as charity.
rows.anchor: ما من امرىء تكون له صلاة بالليل فغلبه عليها نوم فيصلي ما بين طلوع الشمس

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Muslim reports Umar from the Prophet: whoever sleeps through his regular nightly portion may read it between dawn and noon and receive the reward as if reading at night.
rows.anchor: من نام عن حزبه أو عن شيء منه فقرأه فيما بين صلاة الفجر وصلاة الظهر

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi quotes Dhu al-Shahid al-Akbar: people’s created completeness is life and knowledge, but sleep, bodily needs, and physical deficiency afflict them; a person should reduce sleep through restraint and worship where possible.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى خلق العبد حيا عالما، وبذلك كماله، وسلط عليه آفة النوم

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi calculates that a sixty-year life spent sleeping half the night and a sixth of the day wastes two thirds, leaving twenty years, and calls it folly to spend that much life in fleeting pleasure rather than lasting worship.
rows.anchor: ومن الغبن العظيم أن يعيش الرجل ستين سنة ينام ليلها فيذهب النصف من عمره لغوا

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says things do not differ in rank by themselves but by qualities; which is superior, night or day, is disputed, with fasting enough to indicate the answer.
rows.anchor: الأشياء لا تتفاضل بأنفسها فإن الجواهر والأعراض من حيث الوجود متماثلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night has great merit: the Prophet was commanded to pray at night, believers are praised for rising from their beds, and a report praises late prayer, a time when supplications are answered, and the Lord’s descent.
rows.anchor: والليل عظيم قدره أمر نبيه عليه الصلاة والسلام بقيامه فقال

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Hamza, as well as Ibn Waththab, Talha, and al-Nakhaʿi, reads yadhkur with a still dhāl and ḍamma on kaf; the Ubay codex adds a tāʾ, and the remaining readers use a doubled kaf, all with similar meaning.
rows.anchor: بسكون الذال وضم الكاف. وهي قراءة ابن وثاب وطلحة والنخعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lightened reading may mean recalling in one time what was missed in the other, or remembering God’s transcendence and praising Him during both periods.
rows.anchor: بالتخفيف أي يذكر ما نسيه في أحد الوقتين في الوقت الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shukūr is an intensive verbal noun meaning the same as shukr, like kufūr and kufr; the cycles of night and day sustain people’s livelihood and prompt gratitude.
rows.anchor: يقال: شكر يشكر شكرا وشكورا، مثل كفر يكفر كفرا وكفورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The close connects the signs to the question “what is the Merciful?”: He is the One able to make these things.
rows.anchor: قالوا: هو الذي يقدر على هذه الأشياء
